Overview

Generate Music with AI is a full-stack web application that turns a text prompt into an original music track using large language models and serverless GPU inference. You describe the vibe — "lo-fi hip hop with rain ambiance" or "aggressive metalcore with a jazz breakdown" — and the app composes something that didn't exist a moment before.

The project started as an experiment to close the loop between natural language and audio generation. Rather than wrapping a simple API call in a form, I wanted to build the full production-quality system: input validation, rate limiting, async job polling, streaming audio playback, and a UI that responds gracefully to the latency inherent in GPU inference.

How It Works

The user fills out a prompt form on the Next.js frontend and submits. From there, every layer has a specific job:

s out a prompt form on the Next.js frontend and submits. From there, every layer has a specific job: 1. FastAPI backend (Railway) receives the request, validates input, checks rate limits using  with session-cookie keying, then proxies the payload to the ACE-Step API running on Modal.
2. Modal spins up a GPU worker, runs the music generation model, and returns a  immediately — the job is asynchronous.
3. Frontend polls  at an interval until the job completes, showing a live progress indicator.
4. Audio delivery: once complete, the frontend fetches the audio stream from  and renders it in a WaveSurfer.js waveform player.

The backend is a stateless proxy — no audio data is stored server-side. Every request is forwarded to Modal and the response is passed back. This keeps the Railway deployment lightweight and cheap.

Technical Architecture

The architecture is deliberately layered to separate concerns cleanly:

Key engineering decisions:

The architecture is deliberately layered to separate concerns cleanly:

Key engineering decisions: - HTTP/2 with httpx: The  is instantiated once at startup via FastAPI's lifespan context and shared across all requests. This avoids TCP handshake overhead on every generation request and enables multiplexed connections to Modal.
- Session-based rate limiting: Rate limits key on the session cookie and fall back to IP, which prevents one user from exhausting another's quota while handling clients behind shared NAT correctly.
- Typed API client: The Next.js frontend uses a hand-rolled typed fetch wrapper with Zod validation for all API responses. API errors surface as  instances with structured context rather than raw exceptions.
- Job polling over WebSockets: Modal's ACE-Step API uses a job queue model. Polling was simpler to implement correctly and debug than maintaining a persistent WebSocket connection through a serverless reverse proxy.

Skills Demonstrated This project touches every layer of a modern AI-integrated web application — from GPU inference orchestration down to waveform rendering. The engineering decisions were practical ones: stateless proxy to minimize Railway costs, shared HTTP client to reduce latency, typed API contract to catch integration bugs early. Building this sharpened my ability to design systems that are observable, cost-conscious, and handle async complexity without leaking it to the user.

Overview

Baby Name Popularity is an interactive data application for exploring 145 years of US baby name trends from the Social Security Administration, with machine learning models that forecast future name popularity. You can search any name, compare multiple names side by side, browse top names by gender and decade, and see a model-generated popularity prediction for the next several years.

The project grew from a simple question: is a name getting more or less popular, and will that trend continue? The SSA publishes name data going back to 1880, but raw data files are not interactive. Building this meant designing a data pipeline, training and evaluating multiple forecasting models, and wrapping it all in a UI that makes the analysis accessible.

Data Pipeline

e forecasting models, and wrapping it all in a UI that makes the analysis accessible.

Data Pipeline The SSA doesn't offer a direct API download — the data comes as a ZIP archive from a web page that requires JavaScript rendering. The pipeline handles this with Selenium to automate the download, then processes all ~145 annual text files into a single normalized dataset.

For each name-sex-year combination, the pipeline computes:

-  — raw number of births with that name
-  — count as a fraction of all births that year and sex, correcting for population growth
-  — ranking within year and sex (1 = most popular)

Relative metrics matter more than raw counts here: Jennifer peaked at 3.4% of all female births in 1947, which is a more meaningful measure of cultural dominance than the absolute number. The processed data is stored in a SQLite database for fast query access from the Streamlit app.

Machine Learning Models

Machine Learning Models The forecasting task is time-series prediction: given a name's historical popularity trajectory, predict its popularity in future years. The pipeline trains and evaluates four models on this task:

- Linear Regression — fast, interpretable baseline
- Random Forest — captures non-linear relationships between features
- XGBoost — gradient-boosted trees, generally the strongest performer on tabular time series
- LSTM — recurrent neural network for modeling sequential dependencies over long windows

Feature engineering is the core of each model. Rather than feeding raw time series to the models, the pipeline constructs:

- 5-year lookback windows for popularity percentage, total count, and rank
- Linear trend features (slope over recent years)
- Volatility features (standard deviation of recent popularity)
- Normalized year (to handle the full 1880–2024 range)

- Normalized year (to handle the full 1880–2024 range) Models are evaluated by RMSE on a held-out test set, and the best-performing model is persisted with joblib for serving. The pipeline includes a full comparison report so the tradeoffs between models are transparent.

Skills Demonstrated

This project demonstrates the full data science lifecycle: raw data acquisition (web scraping under JavaScript rendering), data engineering (multi-file parsing, normalization, SQLite storage), feature engineering for time series forecasting, comparative model evaluation, and interactive visualization. The choice to train and compare four different model families — rather than jumping straight to XGBoost — reflects how I approach model selection: empirically, with reproducible evaluation, rather than by default.

Overview

Diamonds: Predicting Price is a regression analysis project that models diamond prices from physical and quality attributes using a combination of statistical analysis in R and machine learning in Python. The analysis covers a dataset of ~54,000 diamonds with features including carat weight, cut grade, color grade, clarity grade, and physical dimensions (length, width, depth).

This was my earliest end-to-end data science project. I'm including it here not as a showcase of technical sophistication, but as evidence of where I started — and because the analytical thinking it required is genuinely interesting.

The Analysis The central challenge is that diamond price is not linear in any single feature. Carat weight has the strongest correlation with price, but two diamonds with the same carat weight can differ in price by an order of magnitude based on cut, color, and clarity. These quality grades interact with each other and with size in complex ways.

The analysis proceeded in several phases:

Exploratory data analysis: Distribution analysis revealed that carat weight clusters at round values (0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5) due to market conventions. Price distributions are right-skewed. Log transformation of price and carat improves model fit substantially and is a standard approach in gemological pricing models.

Feature engineering: The raw quality grades (cut: Fair → Ideal, color: J → D, clarity: I1 → IF) are ordinal categories with non-uniform spacing. Encoding them as ordered numerics with interaction terms between carat and quality captures more of the pricing structure than one-hot encoding alone.

terms between carat and quality captures more of the pricing structure than one-hot encoding alone. Modeling: The analysis compared multiple regression approaches — from basic OLS through regularized regression (Ridge, Lasso) to ensemble methods — evaluating each by RMSE and R² on a held-out test set. The log-linear model on transformed features served as the interpretable baseline; gradient boosting models captured the non-linear interactions more accurately at the cost of interpretability.

What I Learned

The most important thing this project taught me wasn't a modeling technique — it was that the structure of the prediction problem determines which features matter and how they should be encoded. Raw carat weight and price look exponentially related. Log-transformed, they look linear. That insight changed how I think about preprocessing: transformation isn't just normalization, it's a way of encoding domain knowledge into the model's feature space.

on isn't just normalization, it's a way of encoding domain knowledge into the model's feature space. This project also gave me an appreciation for the difference between correlation and causal structure. The data shows that Ideal cut diamonds are sometimes cheaper than Fair cut diamonds of the same carat weight. This seems counterintuitive until you realize that buyers seeking large stones (high carat) are often willing to sacrifice cut quality — the feature interactions tell a story about market behavior, not just gemology.

Overview

Chat with Nietzsche is a conversational AI that channels Friedrich Nietzsche's philosophical voice using Retrieval-Augmented Generation over his complete written works. You can ask it about the Will to Power, Eternal Recurrence, master-slave morality, or why it thinks modern social media would have disgusted him — and get answers grounded in Nietzsche's actual writings, with source citations to the passages used.

The goal was never to make a philosophical trivia bot. It was to build a system where responses are demonstrably faithful to the source material. Every answer the system produces can be traced back to real text from the 19 works in the corpus.

The RAG Pipeline

The retrieval pipeline is multi-stage, designed to maximize the quality of context passed to the LLM rather than relying on the model alone.

esigned to maximize the quality of context passed to the LLM rather than relying on the model alone. 1. Query expansion: Philosophical terminology is expanded to related concepts before retrieval — "Übermensch" maps to related ideas like self-overcoming, will to power, and the slave revolt in morality. 2. Multi-query generation: The LLM reformulates the user's question three different ways. Each reformulation is used for independent retrieval, then results are merged. This captures relevant passages that a single query might miss. 3. Hybrid search: Each query hits both a FAISS semantic index (70% weight) and a BM25 keyword index (30% weight). Semantic search handles conceptual overlap; BM25 ensures exact philosophical terms like "Ressentiment" or "Zarathustra" are matched precisely. 4. Cross-encoder re-ranking: Retrieved passages are re-ranked using , a cross-encoder model that scores each passage against the original question jointly, not independently. This separates genuinely relevant passages from those that merely share vocabulary. 5.

ndependently. This separates genuinely relevant passages from those that merely share vocabulary. 5. Grounded generation: The top 5 re-ranked passages are passed to  via Groq. Temperature is set to 0.3 — low enough to suppress creative invention, high enough to avoid robotic phrasing.

re is set to 0.3 — low enough to suppress creative invention, high enough to avoid robotic phrasing. Technical Implementation

Corpus and chunking: All 19 works were sourced from Project Gutenberg public domain translations. Text is split at paragraph boundaries with a 1200-character target and 150-character overlap. Paragraph-based chunking preserves argumentative flow — Nietzsche's writing often builds meaning across a full paragraph, and mid-sentence splits would corrupt the context.

Embeddings:  generates 768-dimensional dense vectors for each chunk. The same model embeds user queries at inference time, ensuring semantic alignment between document and query spaces.

Stack: LangChain orchestrates the retrieval chain. FAISS stores the dense index. BM25 (rank-bm25) handles the sparse index. Both indexes are built locally and committed to the repo, so Streamlit Cloud cold-starts don't require re-indexing.

Source citations: The UI surfaces the specific Nietzsche passages used to generate each response in an expandable section below the answer. This transparency serves two purposes: it lets users verify authenticity, and it demonstrates that the retrieval pipeline found genuinely relevant context rather than hallucinating.

Skills Demonstrated

This project required implementing every component of an advanced RAG pipeline from first principles — no managed vector database, no off-the-shelf retrieval API. The multi-query and cross-encoder stages reflect real production RAG patterns used in enterprise retrieval systems. Deploying it on Streamlit Cloud for free, with a corpus and indexes committed to the repo, demonstrates cost-aware deployment thinking — a skill that matters as much in early-stage AI products as in large enterprises.
